lessons.outcome_text:
Recognise that a cell is a basic unit of life.
Explain that living things reproduce to ensure continuity of their kind and that many characteristics are passed from parents to offspring.
Describe sexual reproduction in flowering plants: pollination, fertilisation (seed production), seed dispersal and germination.
Recognise fertilisation in human sexual reproduction: a sperm fuses with an egg; the fertilised egg develops in the womb; ovaries produce eggs and testes produce sperms.
Recognise the similarity in fertilisation in flowering plants and humans.
Investigate plant reproduction by spores and seeds.
objectives: Explain why living things reproduce.
Describe the sequence of sexual reproduction in flowering plants.
Explain fertilisation in flowering plants and humans at the required level.
Compare reproduction by spores and seeds.

sections.heading: Why reproduction matters
sections.content: Living things reproduce to ensure that their kind continues. Offspring inherit many characteristics from their parents. A cell is the basic unit of life.

sections.heading: Flowering plant reproduction
sections.content: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. After pollination, fertilisation occurs when the male reproductive cell fuses with the female reproductive cell. Seeds form; seeds may be dispersed away from the parent plant.

sections.heading: Germination and plant reproduction
sections.content: Germination is the growth of a seed into a young plant under suitable conditions. Some plants reproduce using spores; others reproduce using seeds.

sections.heading: Human fertilisation
sections.content: The ovaries produce eggs and the testes produce sperms. Fertilisation occurs when a sperm fuses with an egg. The fertilised egg develops in the womb. The syllabus does not require detailed foetal development.

key_takeaways: Explain why living things reproduce.
Describe the sequence of sexual reproduction in flowering plants.
Explain fertilisation in flowering plants and humans at the required level.
Compare reproduction by spores and seeds.

sections.heading: Fertilisation

sections.heading: Spores and seeds

Understand melting point of ice/freezing point of water and boiling point of water.
Explain the roles of evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and recognise its importance.
Investigate the effect of heat gain or loss on water temperature and state, and factors affecting evaporation rate: wind, temperature and exposed surface area.
Recognise the importance of water to life processes and describe impacts of water pollution on Earth's water resources.
objectives: Describe the three states of water and changes between them.
Explain the water cycle using evaporation and condensation.
Interpret simple investigations about evaporation.
Explain why clean water is important and how pollution affects water resources.

sections.heading: Three states of water
sections.content: Water can exist as solid ice, liquid water and water vapour (a gas). These states can change into one another when heat is gained or lost.

sections.heading: Changes of state
sections.content: Melting changes ice to liquid water at 0°C. Freezing changes water to ice at 0°C. Water boils at 100°C under normal atmospheric pressure. Evaporation can occur at temperatures below boiling. Condensation changes water vapour into liquid water.

sections.heading: The water cycle
sections.content: Water evaporates from surfaces. Water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds. Water returns to Earth as precipitation and collects in water bodies. Evaporation and condensation are key processes.

sections.heading: Investigating evaporation
sections.content: Wind, higher temperature and a larger exposed surface area increase the rate of evaporation. In a fair test, change one factor and keep the others the same.

sections.heading: Water and life
sections.content: Water is needed for life processes. Pollution can make water unsafe and reduce the amount of usable water. Conserving water helps protect this limited natural resource.

key_takeaways: Describe the three states of water and changes between them.
Explain the water cycle using evaporation and condensation.
Interpret simple investigations about evaporation.
Explain why clean water is important and how pollution affects water resources.

sections.heading: Three states
sections.content: Water exists as solid ice, liquid water and water vapour (gas).

sections.heading: Changes of state
sections.content: Melting: ice to water. Freezing: water to ice. Boiling: water to steam at 100°C. Condensation: water vapour to liquid water. Ice melts and water freezes at 0°C.

sections.heading: Water cycle
sections.content: Water evaporates, water vapour condenses to form clouds, and water returns to Earth. The cycle is important because it moves water through the environment.

sections.heading: Conserving water
sections.content: Water is a limited natural resource. We can reduce waste by turning off taps and using water carefully.

Compare how plants, fish and humans take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
Compare transport in plants and humans: plant tubes transport food and water; human blood vessels transport digested food, oxygen and carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: Air and breathing
sections.content: Air is a mixture of gases. It contains mainly nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller amounts of carbon dioxide and water vapour. The nose, windpipe and lungs are parts of the respiratory system.

sections.heading: Respiratory system
sections.content: Air enters through the nose, travels down the windpipe and reaches the lungs. Oxygen from inhaled air enters the body; carbon dioxide is removed when we breathe out.

sections.heading: Circulatory system
sections.content: The heart pumps blood around the body. Blood vessels carry blood. Blood transports oxygen and digested food to body parts and carries carbon dioxide away.

sections.heading: Systems work together
sections.content: The digestive system provides digested food, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, and the circulatory system transports these substances to cells. These systems work together to support life.

sections.heading: Comparing living things
sections.content: Plants, fish and humans take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide in different ways. In plants, tubes transport water and food. In humans, blood vessels transport digested food, oxygen and carbon dioxide.

key_takeaways: Identify major parts and functions of respiratory and circulatory systems.
Explain how oxygen enters the body and is transported.

sections.heading: Air
sections.content: Air is a mixture of gases. It contains nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.

sections.heading: Breathing system
sections.content: The nose, windpipe and lungs are parts of the respiratory system. They help air enter and leave the body.

sections.heading: Blood circulation

sections.heading: Plants are systems
sections.content: A plant has parts that work together. Roots absorb water. Leaves make food. The plant transport system moves water and food to where they are needed.

sections.heading: Transporting water
sections.content: Water absorbed by the roots is transported through water-carrying tubes to other parts of the plant, including the leaves.

sections.heading: Transporting food
sections.content: Food made in the leaves is transported through food-carrying tubes to other parts of the plant for growth and other life processes.

sections.heading: Investigating transport
sections.content: A coloured-water investigation can show water movement through a plant stem. Keep the plant, water amount and time consistent when comparing results.

sections.heading: An electrical system
sections.content: A simple electrical system can include a battery, connecting wires, a bulb and a switch. The battery is the energy source.

sections.heading: Open and closed circuits
sections.content: A closed circuit is a complete path that allows current to flow and the bulb to light. An open circuit has a break, so current cannot flow.

sections.heading: Conductors and insulators
sections.content: Conductors allow electricity to pass through them; insulators do not allow electricity to pass through easily. Metals are commonly used as conductors; plastic is commonly used as an insulator.

sections.heading: Changing a circuit
sections.content: Adding batteries in series increases the energy supplied. Adding bulbs in series generally makes each bulb dimmer. In a parallel arrangement, bulbs have separate branches.

sections.heading: Electrical safety
sections.content: Use only low-voltage batteries in classroom investigations. Never experiment with mains electricity. Switch off devices when not in use.

safety_notes: Use low-voltage batteries only. Never use mains electricity.

sections.heading: Circuit parts
sections.content: A simple circuit has a battery, wires, a bulb and sometimes a switch. The battery provides energy.

sections.heading: Closed circuits
sections.content: A closed circuit is a complete path. Current can flow and the bulb lights. If the path is broken, the bulb goes off.

sections.heading: Conductors and insulators
sections.content: Conductors allow electricity to pass through. Insulators do not allow electricity to pass through easily.

sections.heading: Series circuits
sections.content: Batteries and bulbs can be connected in series. Adding batteries can make a bulb brighter. Adding bulbs in series generally makes bulbs dimmer. Use safe low-voltage batteries only.

safety_notes: Use low-voltage batteries only. Never use mains electricity.
